source.notes: SPECIMEN Question Paper for the ICSE 2026 Examination, Chemistry (Science Paper – 2), printed 'T26 522 – SPECIMEN' on every page (used as paperCode). Maximum Marks 80, Time allowed Two hours (120 minutes). Section A (Question 1–2, 40 marks) is compulsory; Section B (Question 3–8, 40 marks) instructs 'Attempt any four questions' out of six, each worth 10 marks — these are six independent, complete questions, NOT internal-choice OR pairs (the paper prints no 'OR' anywhere in Section B), so all six are included here without choiceGroup/part alternatives. Summing every printed mark in this pack therefore totals 100 (40 + 6×10), which is expected and not an error: a candidate only answers 4 of the 6 Section-B questions to reach the printed maximum of 80. The official marking scheme ('ICSE 2026 SPECIMEN DRAFT MARKING SCHEME – CHEMISTRY (SCIENCE PAPER 2)') is printed in the same PDF (pages 16–20) and is itself labelled 'DRAFT' by CISCE; answerSourceUrl is therefore the same URL as sourceUrl and answerSourceFile is null. Question 1's 15 MCQ/assertion-reason sub-parts are each 1 mark (marking scheme marks them '[15x1]'); the printed [15] is the Question-1 total. Cognitive-level tags ('[Recall]'/'[Understanding]'/'[Application]'/'[Analysis]', and compound tags such as '[Understanding & Application]' or '[Recall & Understanding]') are printed in the paper's right margin. Unlike some other ICSE specimens where every lettered sub-part carries its own tag, in THIS document only ONE tag is printed per roman-numeral item — confirmed by inspecting the raw (non-layout) text extraction of every page, which shows exactly one bracketed tag following each item's full block of lettered sub-parts (e.g. Q2(ii)'s five 'Identify the following' sub-items (a)-(e) carry a single trailing '[Recall]'). Where such an item was split into several self-contained lettered entries (because each sub-answer is independently gradable), that one shared tag was applied to every split entry, since only one tag exists for the whole block and there is no ambiguity about which entry it belongs to. Compound tags are recorded verbatim as printed (e.g. cognitiveLevel 'Understanding & Application'), per the instruction to record cognitive tags exactly as printed. The PDF text layer drops the reaction-arrow glyph entirely (extracts as a blank gap) throughout every chemical equation in both the question paper and the marking scheme (confirmed by inspecting the raw bytes around several such gaps in both UTF-8 and Latin-1 extraction — the arrow glyph simply is not present in the text layer, unlike subscripts/superscripts which are extracted flat). Since every such gap sits unambiguously between one reactant block and one product block, it was rebuilt as '→' and flagged per question, with confidence set to MEDIUM for the affected entries — the same treatment the format guide gives to unambiguous fraction/power reconstruction. Chemical formula subscripts came out flat throughout (e.g. H2SO4, CO2, NH4Cl) and are kept as extracted, flagged per question; a few superscripts (e.g. 'Al³+', '10²²') rendered correctly via Unicode superscript characters and needed no flagging. Sub-questions built around a shared stem, diagram or dataset — Q2(i)'s three-step electroplating apparatus, Q3(iii)'s electron-affinity comparison of X and Y, Q4(iii)'s salt-X analysis narrative, Q4(iv)'s esterification set-up, Q6(i)'s two-experiment picture, Q6(iii)'s ammonium dichromate decomposition, Q7(iv)'s pH 2/7/13 solutions, Q8(iii)'s zinc-compound conversion scheme, and Q8(iv)'s elements L/M/N — were kept together as one CASE_BASED/NUMERICAL/SHORT_ANSWER entry with the parts embedded in the text, per the brief, since the parts cannot stand alone without that shared context; each such entry uses the shared block's marks as printed (marksSource PRINTED) rather than guessing a per-part split. Sub-questions that are independently self-contained despite a shared instruction line (e.g. Q2(ii)/(iii) 'Identify the following'/'Complete the following', Q3(i)/(ii) 'observation'/'reasons' pairs, Q3(iv), Q4(i)/(ii), Q5(iii)/(iv), Q6(ii)/(iv), Q7(i)/(ii)/(iii), Q8(i)) were split into separate entries; where the QP/marking scheme give only one combined bracket mark for the group with no per-item breakdown, marksSource is SECTION_INSTRUCTIONS and an even split is assumed (noted per entry); where the marking scheme gives an explicit per-part breakdown (e.g. Q2(v) '[3+2]'), marksSource is PRINTED. Q2(v)(a) (IUPAC names of two unshown organic structures, marking-scheme marks '3') and Q2(v)(b) (draw structural diagrams for three named compounds, marking-scheme marks '2') are each kept as one entry rather than split further, since 3 marks over 2 items and 2 marks over 3 items do not divide evenly and no per-item confirmation exists; Q2(v)(b) has no officialAnswer since the marking scheme's answer is itself an undrawn structural diagram not present in the text layer (same for Q8(ii), 'draw the electron dot diagram of ammonium ion'). Diagrams, a picture and one conversion-scheme table are not reproduced and are flagged per question with hasFigure and extractionIssues: Q1(v) (four unlabelled reactions shown only in a diagram, unanswerable — confidence LOW), Q1(ix) (four hydrocarbon structures shown only in a diagram, unanswerable — confidence LOW), Q1(xi) (a pH-change table flattened by the text layer, reconstructed from the printed row order — confidence MEDIUM), Q1(xv) (an electrorefining-of-copper apparatus diagram; answerable from general knowledge of the process — confidence MEDIUM), Q2(i) (the step-1 electroplating apparatus diagram), Q2(v)(a) (two unshown organic structures, unanswerable — confidence LOW), Q6(i) (a picture showing which solutions are mixed in Experiments 1 and 2; the solutions themselves are not named anywhere in the extracted text, so the question is unanswerable without the figure — confidence LOW), and Q8(iii) (a conversion-scheme diagram for ZnSO4/Zn/ZnS/Zn(OH)2 whose arrows and order are not reliably reconstructable from the flattened text layout — confidence LOW). Every question was mapped to one of the 12 valid chemistry chapter slugs; none required chapter: null.

questions.text:
Electroplating steel objects with silver involves a three-step process.
step 1  A coating of copper is applied to the object.
step 2  A coating of nickel is applied to the object.
step 3  The coating of silver is applied to the object.

(a) A diagram of the apparatus used for step 1 is shown.
1. The chemical process taking place on the surface of the object is Cu2+ (aq) + 2e- → Cu(s). What is the observation seen on the surface of the object?
2. Explain why the concentration of copper ions in the electrolyte remains constant throughout step 1.
(b) Give two changes which would be needed in order to coat nickel onto the object in step 2.
(c) Write down the reaction taking place at the positive electrode during step 3.
extractionIssues: Diagram of the step-1 electroplating apparatus on page 8 (PDF page) not reproduced.
Marking scheme splits the 5 marks as (a)=2 [covering both a.1 and a.2], (b)=2, (c)=1; kept as one case-based entry around the shared three-step scenario and diagram, so the printed [5] is used as-is.
Subscript/superscript flattened in the question and official answer: Cu2+, Ag+, e-.

officialAnswer.text:
(a).1 Reddish brown deposit/ pink deposit/ mass increases
(a).2 As anode released copper ions, the concentration of copper ions does not decrease
(b) Anode should be made up of Nickel and the electrolyte should be aq. Nickel sulphate or any salt solution of Nickel
(c) Ag → Ag+ + e-

questions.text:
Solid ammonium dichromate decomposes as under:
(NH4)2Cr2O7 → N2 + Cr2O3 + 4H2O
If 126 g of ammonium dichromate decomposes, calculate:
(a) the number of moles of ammonium dichromate that undergoes decomposition.
(b) the mass of chromic oxide formed at the same time.
(c) the volume of nitrogen gas evolved at STP.
[At. Wt: N=14, Cr=52, O=16, H=1]
extractionIssues: Subscripts flattened: (NH4)2Cr2O7, N2, Cr2O3, H2O.
Reaction arrow not present in text layer; rendered as → based on layout.

officialAnswer.text:
(a) 252 g of Ammonium dichromate = 1 mole; 126 g of Ammonium dichromate = 0.5 moles
(b) 252 g of ammonium dichromate gives 152 g of chromic oxide; 126 g of ammonium dichromate provides 152×126/252 = 76 g of chromic oxide
(c) 252 g of ammonium dichromate produces 22.4 l of nitrogen; 126 g of ammonium dichromate produces 22.4×126/252 = 11.2 l of nitrogen
